questions.question: You set an environment variable named SECRET_KEY (no prefix) and read it with import.meta.env.SECRET_KEY in your React code. What happens?
options: It works, because Vite exposes all env vars to your code
It is undefined, because only variables starting with VITE_ are exposed to your app's code
It throws a build error that stops the deploy
It works only in development but not in the production build
questions.explanation: Vite only exposes variables prefixed with VITE_ to your app's code; anything without that prefix shows up as undefined in the browser.

questions.question: A teammate adds VITE_API_KEY to Vercel, redeploys, and says 'great, our secret is safe now.' Are they right?
options: Yes, Vercel encrypts all environment variables so they stay hidden
Yes, the VITE_ prefix specifically hides the value from the browser
No, anything with the VITE_ prefix is baked into the JavaScript the browser downloads and can be read in dev tools
No, but only because they forgot to also set it in the local .env file
questions.explanation: The VITE_ prefix guarantees the value lands in code anyone can read, so it is fine for public keys like the Supabase publishable/anon key but never for a true secret.

questions.question: Which Supabase key is designed to be public and safe to put in a VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY variable that ends up in the browser bundle?
options: The service-role key
The database admin key
The publishable key (older projects call it the anon key), protected by Row Level Security
Any key, since the VITE_ prefix encrypts it
questions.explanation: The Supabase publishable key (older projects' anon key) is designed to be public and is protected by Row Level Security, so it is safe in the browser; service-role or admin keys must never get the VITE_ prefix.

questions.question: Clicking a link to /habits/3 inside your deployed app works, but refreshing on /habits/3 returns a 404. Why?
options: Refreshing clears React Router's memory, so the route is lost
Refreshing makes the browser ask the server for a file at /habits/3, which doesn't exist, while clicking is handled in the browser by React Router with no server request
Vercel rate-limits repeated requests to the same path
The chart component fails to load on a hard refresh
questions.explanation: Clicking is handled entirely in the browser by React Router with no server request, but refreshing asks the server for /habits/3, which has no file, so without a rewrite you get a 404.

questions.question: Which vercel.json fixes deep-link 404s for a single-page app by sending unknown paths to index.html?
options: { "redirects": [ { "from": "/index.html", "to": "/(.*)" } ] }
{ "rewrites": [ { "source": "/(.*)", "destination": "/index.html" } ] }
{ "build": { "output": "index.html" } }
{ "routes": [ { "src": "/habits/3", "dest": "/index.html" } ] }
questions.explanation: A rewrite rule mapping /(.*) to /index.html tells Vercel to serve index.html for any unrecognized path and let React Router decide what to show.

questions.question: Why should you keep main always-deployable and build features on branches like add-charts?
options: Because Vercel only deploys branches that are not main
Because Git refuses to merge unless main is clean
Because Vercel deploys main automatically, so keeping main working means half-done work never breaks your live site
Because feature branches run faster builds than main
questions.explanation: Vercel auto-deploys main, so keeping it always in a working state means your live site is never broken by half-finished work while feature branches let you experiment freely.

questions.question: Your app shows a blank white screen for a second before habits appear. Which data-fetch state is missing and why does it matter?
options: The empty state; users with no data assume the app crashed
The error state; a failed request needs a retry button
The loading state; rendering nothing during the fetch reads as 'broken' to users, while a spinner or skeleton signals the app is working
None; a brief blank screen is the expected loading behavior
questions.explanation: During the fetch you're rendering nothing instead of a loading indicator; a blank screen reads as broken, whereas a spinner or skeleton tells users the app is working.

questions.question: Following React Testing Library's 'test how users use it' rule, which is the better test of a menu, and why?
options: Checking 'the isOpen state is true after clicking,' because it inspects the component directly
Checking 'the menu is visible after clicking,' because it tests user-visible behavior and survives refactors of internal state
Checking that a specific CSS class is applied, because classes are stable
Both are equally good as long as they pass
questions.explanation: Testing that the menu is visible checks user-visible behavior, so it stays valid even if you rename or restructure internal state, while asserting on isOpen breaks on harmless refactors and proves nothing about the user experience.
